description: 🚀 AstronXXX is a team of enthusiastic students passionate about space, science, and technology. We are interested in Python, AI/ML, Electronics, data analysis, and problem-solving. We believe in creativity, teamwork, and innovation. We welcome members with skills in programming, web development, UI/UX design, data visualization, research, and presentation. Beginners who are eager to learn and contribute are welcome. Let's innovate beyond boundaries! 🌍
summary:
Earth Information Jukebox: Hear the Arctic Ice Disappear turns NASA satellite-based Arctic sea ice data into sound. We developed an interactive web page where each year is one musical note: a low note means a lot of sea ice, and a high note means less. When you press Play, you hear the pitch climb across more than 45 years of data while a chart marker and live caption show the year and ice extent in million km².

This addresses the challenge by making Earth observation data something people can listen to and explore, not just read in charts. Sound also makes the data more accessible to people who have difficulty with visual graphs.

It matters because Arctic sea ice is a key indicator of climate change, and hearing the decline in under a minute makes it easy to understand and remember. We used the NSIDC Sea Ice Index (derived from NASA satellite observations), Python for data processing, and JavaScript with the Web Audio API for the page, hosted on GitHub Pages. The design can grow to include more Earth datasets as new tracks.
details:
What it does and how it works
Earth Information Jukebox turns Arctic sea ice data into sound. I used the NSIDC Sea Ice Index (based on NASA satellite observations) and kept the September extent for each year from 1979 onward, which is the yearly minimum. Each value is mapped to a pitch: more ice gives a low note (220 Hz), and less ice gives a high note (880 Hz). When a user presses Play, each year is played as one note while a chart marker moves along the data and a live caption shows the year and ice extent in million km². The pitch climbs as the ice shrinks.

Benefits and intended impact

  • It makes a long climate record understandable in under a minute.
  • It gives people who cannot easily read charts another way to explore Earth data.
  • It helps students and the public connect with NASA data emotionally, not just numerically.
  • It works in any browser with one button, with no installation or technical knowledge.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: NSIDC Sea Ice Index, monthly extent by year (Northern Hemisphere)
  • Python (Pandas, NumPy, SciPy) in Google Colab to clean the data and test the sound
  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript with the Web Audio API for the interactive page
  • GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting the code and live demo
  • Google Colab for running the data processing
  • An AI assistant (Claude) helped me plan the project, write and debug code, and draft documentation. I ran, tested and deployed the project myself.

Creativity
Instead of another chart, I treated data as music. The “jukebox” idea means each Earth dataset can become a track, and Arctic ice is the first song. Using the ear to notice a trend is a different way to experience satellite data.

Factors I considered

  • Clarity: low means more ice and high means less ice, so the direction is easy to understand.
  • Accuracy: pitch shows relative change, so the caption always displays the real value. The data source and units are credited.
  • Accessibility: sound adds a non-visual way to explore the data.
  • Simplicity: one dataset and one button, built to be reliable.
  • Limitations: this is a prototype with one track, September values only, and extent rather than ice thickness. Future work includes more tracks (Antarctic ice, sea surface temperature), NASA satellite imagery, and user controls.
